title: 'If this was a bylaw infraction, how does it end up in a death?': Family friend speaks out on SIU report into death of Moses Erhirhie, who was shot by police officer in Markham
article: A friend of Moses Erhirhie's family is speaking out in the wake of the Special Investigations Unit clearing the officer who shot Erhirhie of criminal charges.
Erhirhie was shot by a York Regional Police officer on Jan. 22, 2022 after an interaction that began when he was spotted possibly urinating on a snow bank in Markham

On Jan. 11, the provincial police watchdog released a report into the shooting that answered a number of important questions about the deadly incident, while leaving several other key questions that arose unanswered.
Many of these unanswered questions came to the fore as a result of the officer involved electing not to speak or hand over his notes to investigators, as is his legal right.

"My heart was broken when I read the report," David Bosveld, a friend of the Erhirhie family and a community organizer, said. "How could someone have, what for most people would be a meaningless interaction with a police officer, and wind up dead?"

With use of videos obtained from the shopping plaza at Hwy. 7 and Fairburn Drive and a witness, SIU investigators found the officer pulled up behind Erhirhie's vehicle before the two engaged in a conversation.
The officer got out of the cruiser and went to Erhirhie's vehicle, in which a woman sat in the passenger seat, and there was a scuffle when Erhirhie reached for the driver's side door handle.
When Erhirhie managed to get into the vehicle, he accelerated backward onto the snowbank with his door open and the officer partially inside.
When the vehicle came to a stop, the officer got out and shot Erhirhie "up to" three times, the SIU report states.

"It appeared (Erhirhie) was attempting to exit the Hyundai via the open front passenger door when he was struck by one or more of the gunshots and collapsed - his head coming to rest on the front passenger seat, his feet on the driver's seat," the report reads.
An autopsy showed three bullets struck Erhirhie.
In the aftermath, the report says a gun was found in a satchel on Erhirhie's person, and the woman was arrested before eventually being released without charge.
Bosveld said the fact the officer is not required to speak to the SIU is extra difficult for the family to swallow.

"How broken will the family, who are seeking truth, accountability and justice, be to find out the officer who shot and killed their family member wasn't obliged to provide an explanation for any part of that interaction?" he said.
In his analysis of the decision, director Joseph Martino questioned why the officer tried to detain Erhirhie.

"Had (Erhirhie) refused to identify himself so that a ticket could be issued, thereby leaving himself open to lawful arrest?" he wrote. "The answers to these questions are important. If the (officer) had no lawful reason to arrest or detain the Complainant, then the Complainant was entitled to resist that process."
Nicholas Charitsis, a criminal defence attorney in Toronto, said not being obliged to speak is a fundamental right in Canada that should not be treated lightly.

"If the officer had reached out to me and told me the situation ... I would have forcefully advised him not to say anything," Charitsis said. "If law enforcement asks you questions, you must only identify yourself. You are not obliged to say anything else. It's the first thing you learn in law school ... the right to remain silent."

Bosveld further criticized the SIU for how long the investigation took - almost one year - and the fact the organization left so many questions unanswered, including why the officer tried to apprehend Erhirhie when it's possible the only infraction Erhirhie committed was a bylaw infraction. He said he doesn't believe the SIU is fit for service.

"The SIU is not an effective tool at holding officers to account when these types of situations occur," he said. "We need real oversight and this is not that. If this was issuing a bylaw infraction, then how did this end up in a death?"

A spokesperson for the watchdog, Monica Hudon, said the SIU's report was delayed as it awaited the autopsy examination from the coroner's office and insisted that when there is evidence that a criminal offence has been committed, the SIU will lay charges.

"Subject officials are invited, but not compelled, to present themselves for an interview with the SIU and they do not have to submit their notes to the SIU," she wrote in an email. "Once (the officer) becomes the focus of an investigation and therefore under criminal jeopardy, the subject official is granted the same rights as any citizen under the Charter of Rights and Freedoms to protect (the officer) from self-incrimination."
Bosveld did not comment on whether there will be a civil suit against the officer or human rights case on the back of the SIU report.
York Regional Police did not respond to a request for comment about whether the officer will face any subsequent internal investigation.
When asked to comment on whether it means anything to him that the officer is, according to a source, Black, Bosveld said it did not.

"When people become police, they join a blue brotherhood and what we see is people, regardless of their race, being consumed by the police culture," he said. "So, no, it's not surprising to see an officer act in this fashion."
